scenario.name: Mandiant, Wiz & Google Cloud — GCP iam.serviceAccountKeys.create & serviceAccounts.actAs Impersonation Escalation
scenario.shortSubtitle: Mandiant · Wiz · Rhino Security Labs · iam.serviceAccountKeys.create · Default Compute SA Editor Pivot & GCS Exfil
scenario.overview: Imagine an underground city subway metro station with tiled tunnel walls, glowing route maps, chrome fare turnstiles, ticket kiosks, and a gleaming metro train sliding along the platform. Down in the underground subway concourse, a rider taps a replayed magnetic metro fare card at the chrome turnstile bank during evening rush hour. In this real-world scenario, the intruder bypasses the normal inspection rule to reach the underground subway train car, then smuggles copied records out past the metro card turnstile bank in tiny disguised batches. The metro booth attendant’s fare-gate console flags a single card swiped at two distant stations within seconds and alerts transit security. In this scenario (T1098.001, Mandiant, Wiz & Google Cloud, GCP iam.serviceAccountKeys.create & serviceAccounts.actAs Impersonation Escalation), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: discovering the Over-Privileged Default, then minting a Persistent User-Managed JSON Key, then activating loot_key.json Outside GCP. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Discovering the Over-Privileged Default, then Minting a Persistent User-Managed JSON Key, then Activating loot_key.json Outside GCP, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 1 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: ENUMERATING PRIVILEGED DEFAULT COMPUTE SERVICE ACCOUNT
stages.subtitle: Identifying 482910492810-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com with project-wide roles/editor
stages.description: Down in the underground subway concourse, a rider taps a replayed magnetic metro fare card at the chrome turnstile bank during evening rush hour. Specifically in Step 1, the intruder bypasses the normal inspection rule to reach the underground subway train car while everyday visitors and the metro station agent go about their routine. Using a compromised low-privilege CI service account (ci-runner@corp-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com), the attacker runs gcloud iam service-accounts list (calling google.iam.admin.v1.ListServiceAccounts) and identifies 482910492810-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com (the Default Compute Engine Service Account that GCP automatically creates and historically binds to the primitive role roles/editor, granting read/write access to almost every service in the project). As Wiz Research documented, unless an organization explicitly enables constraints/iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts, newly created Compute Engine and App Engine default service accounts receive project-wide Editor rights. In the documented GCP ADMIN_ACTIVITY exchange from Compromised GCP Workload Caller to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with RESP HTTP 200 (confirming that the LIST_SERVICE_ACCOUNTS request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 MINTING USER-MANAGED RSA JSON KEY VIA CREATESERVICEACCOUNTKEY). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ LIST_SERVICE_ACCOUNTS / ⇠#1 RESP HTTP 200) from Node ① (#1 Compromised GCP Workload Caller) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Google Cloud SCC & Chronicle SIEM).

stages.title: MINTING USER-MANAGED RSA JSON KEY VIA CREATESERVICEACCOUNTKEY
stages.subtitle: Calling google.iam.admin.v1.CreateServiceAccountKey to download a persistent private key
stages.description: The turnstile arm clicks open, letting the rider step onto the platform and slip through the driver’s unlocked service door at the front of the subway car. Here in Step 2 inside the subway metro, the intruder quietly copies a trusted access pass from the metro station agent's station without disturbing the emergency exit stairs. Because the ci-runner identity holds roles/iam.serviceAccountKeyAdmin (which includes iam.serviceAccountKeys.create) scoped at the project level rather than restricted to a single non-privileged account, the attacker runs gcloud iam service-accounts keys create loot_key.json --iam-account=482910492810-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com (causing GCP IAM to generate a 2048-bit RSA key pair, store the public key on the Default Compute Service Account, and download the PKCS#8 private key in loot_key.json to the attacker’s machine). Unlike short-lived metadata tokens on a GCE VM, a user-managed service account key JSON file does not expire for 10 years by default and can be used from anywhere on the internet unless blocked by VPC Service Controls. In the documented GCP CreateServiceAccountKey exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to GCP IAM Control Plane API, GCP IAM Control Plane API responds with ALERT KEY_ID 9f8e7d6c5b (confirming that the USER_MANAGED_SA_KEY_CREATED request succeeded on GCP IAM Control Plane API and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 IMPERSONATED EDITOR AUTHENTICATION & GCS BUCKET EXFILTRATION). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ USER_MANAGED_SA_KEY_CREATED / ⇠#2 ALERT KEY_ID 9f8e7d6c5b) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 GCP IAM Control Plane API), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Google Cloud SCC & Chronicle SIEM).

stages.title: IMPERSONATED EDITOR AUTHENTICATION & GCS BUCKET EXFILTRATION
stages.subtitle: Activating loot_key.json to inherit roles/editor and bulk-download gs://corp-financial-ledger-prod
stages.description: Inside the subway cab, the intruder reads the station relay schedule and triggers an unauthorized express skip past the next inspection stop. In this final step inside the subway metro, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the metro card turnstile bank in tiny disguised batches until the fare-gate audit console catches the mismatch. The attacker runs gcloud auth activate-service-account --key-file=loot_key.json (which signs a JWT assertion locally with the RSA private key and exchanges it at oauth2.googleapis.com/token for a 1-hour OAuth2 access token ya29.* carrying the Default Compute Service Account’s roles/editor permissions) and executes gcloud storage cp -r gs://corp-financial-ledger-prod ./dump/ to exfiltrate 8,900 financial Parquet files. In GCP Data Access audit logs, when a Compute Engine service account authenticates via a downloaded JSON key rather than the internal GCE metadata server, authenticationInfo.serviceAccountKeyName is populated with the exact key ID, giving defenders a 100% deterministic indicator of key theft. In the documented GCP DATA_ACCESS storage.objects.get exchange from GCP IAM Control Plane API to Default Compute Service Account, Default Compute Service Account responds with RESP 8,900 Objects Read (confirming that the GCS_BULK_DOWNLOAD request succeeded on Default Compute Service Account and completing the final execution objective of Mandiant, Wiz & Google Cloud, GCP iam.serviceAccountKeys.create & serviceAccounts.actAs Impersonation Escalation). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ GCS_BULK_DOWNLOAD / ⇠#3 RESP 8,900 Objects Read) from Node ③ (#3 GCP IAM Control Plane API) to Node ④ (#4 Default Compute Service Account), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Google Cloud SCC & Chronicle SIEM).

detectionRule.title: GCP Default Compute Service Account Authenticated Using Static Key Outside GCE
detectionRule.ruleCode: gcp_cloudaudit_data_access | where principalEmail endswith "-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com" and isnotempty(serviceAccountKeyName)
detectionRule.mitigation: Delete all user-managed keys on *-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com and alert whenever serviceAccountKeyName is non-empty.
